title: Unit 2 Quiz · Data Preparation & Exploration
instructions: 33 questions, 34 marks. You have 30 minutes; the quiz submits itself when time runs out.
Questions and options are shuffled, so your neighbour's screen will not match yours.
Multi-select questions need ALL correct options for the marks. Ordering questions give part marks for each item in the right place.
After submitting you will see your score and an explanation for every question.

questions.q: Data collected earlier for a different purpose, such as billing records reused for a churn study, is called:
questions.explain: Secondary data was collected for another purpose. Primary data is collected for your exact question.

questions.q: The ticket file has one row per complaint (1,840 rows). Before joining it to a one-row-per-customer table you should:
options: Aggregate it to one count per customer
questions.explain: Joining at the wrong grain copies each customer once per ticket. Group by customer first (tickets.groupby(...).size()).

questions.q: The CRM has 1,500 customers; the usage file covers 1,475 of them. Which join keeps all 1,500 customers?
questions.explain: A left join keeps every row of the left table. An inner join would silently drop the 25 customers with no usage record.

questions.q: 10 usage rows have IDs like “st10007” while the CRM uses “ST10007”. What happens if you join without fixing this?
options: Those 10 customers get no usage data
The join fails with an error
Nothing; IDs are compared ignoring case
questions.explain: String keys must match exactly. Standardise keys (e.g. .str.upper()) before joining.

questions.q: Arrange these cleaning steps in a sensible order.
options: Read the raw file as text
questions.explain: Read safely, de-duplicate before counting anything, standardise so keys and labels match, join, then check values in the combined table.

questions.q: “Prepaid”, “prepaid”, “Pre-paid” and “PREPAID” all appear in plan_type. Which data-quality dimension is this?
questions.explain: The same thing written different ways is a consistency problem. It splits one group into several.

questions.q: Which pandas code turns “₹399” and “399.00” into the number 399.0?
questions.explain: Remove the symbol, then convert. astype(int) would fail on “₹399” and on “399.00”.

questions.q: Why should exact duplicates be removed BEFORE computing the churn rate?
options: Otherwise duplicated customers are counted twice
pandas cannot compute rates with duplicates
questions.explain: Every statistic computed before de-duplication counts the copies again, biasing rates and averages.

questions.q: Age is missing for 6.0% of prepaid customers but 1.4% of postpaid customers. This missingness is best described as:
questions.explain: It depends on another column we know (plan type): Missing At Random given that column.

questions.q: Customers who are unhappy skip the satisfaction survey. This missingness is:
questions.explain: The gap depends on the very value that is missing (low satisfaction): Missing Not At Random.

questions.q: 1,436 observed ages have sd 10.22. After filling 64 gaps with the mean, the sd becomes:
questions.explain: The filled values sit on the mean and add nothing to Σ(x − x̄)², so sd = 10.22 × √(1435/1499) ≈ 10.00.

questions.q: Why add an “age_was_missing” column before filling the gaps?
options: So the model can still use the fact that the value was missing
questions.explain: If missingness carries information (MAR/MNAR), the flag preserves it after imputation.

questions.q: A customer with no support ticket in the ticket file should get support_calls =
questions.explain: No ticket means zero calls: a known fact, not an unknown value. Imputing an average would invent complaints.

questions.q: data_gb has Q1 = 21.90 and Q3 = 43.65. What is the upper IQR fence (1.5 rule)?
With mean 37.76 and sd 59.18, what is the z-score of a 999.9 GB reading?
Six huge glitches inflate the standard deviation, so genuine heavy users no longer reach |z| > 3. This effect is called:
questions.explain: Outliers distort the mean and sd that the z rule depends on, hiding other outliers. The IQR rule is more robust.

questions.q: A monthly charge of ₹59,900 appears where all plans cost ₹199–₹999, and the billing team confirms it was ₹599. Best treatment:
options: Replace it with the mean charge
questions.explain: An error you can explain and correct should be corrected, not deleted or averaged away.

questions.q: In a fraud-detection project, extremely unusual transactions should usually be:
options: Kept, because they may be the very cases you want to detect
questions.explain: In fraud and anomaly detection the outliers are the signal.

questions.q: Monthly charges range from ₹199 to ₹999. What is the min-max scaled value of ₹599?
Mean charge is ₹474.55 and sd ₹211.44. What is the z-score of ₹599?
Which model does NOT need its features scaled?
questions.explain: Trees split on one feature at a time using thresholds, so scale does not matter. Distance- and gradient-based models need scaling.

questions.q: Voice minutes are strongly right-skewed (skew 1.39). Which transformation helps most?
questions.explain: A log transform compresses large values more than small ones; skew fell from 1.39 to −0.60. Scaling does not change the shape.

questions.q: Payment mode (UPI, Card, Cash, Net banking) should be encoded with:
questions.explain: Nominal categories have no order; ordinal codes would invent one.

questions.q: City tier (Tier-1, Tier-2, Tier-3) can sensibly be encoded as:
questions.explain: City tier has a natural order, so ordinal encoding preserves it.

questions.q: Which of these is a FILTER feature-selection method?
questions.explain: Filters score each feature on its own. RFE and forward selection are wrappers; L1 is embedded.

questions.q: Monthly charge and data_gb have r = 0.91. What should you usually do?
options: Keep one of them; they carry nearly the same information
Keep both; more features are always better
questions.explain: Highly correlated predictors are redundant (multicollinearity) and make coefficients unstable.

questions.q: For plan type vs churn, χ² = 12.96 with 1 degree of freedom (5% critical value 3.84). Conclusion:
options: Plan type and churn are related; keep the feature
They are independent; drop the feature
questions.explain: 12.96 > 3.84 (p = 0.0003), so we reject independence. The test shows association, not causation.

questions.q: Expected count for Postpaid & Churn = Yes: 566 postpaid customers, 340 churners, 1,500 customers in total.
questions.explain: Expected = row total × column total ÷ grand total = 566 × 340 / 1500 = 128.29.

questions.q: Why should feature selection be done on the training data only?
options: Using the test set to choose features leaks information and inflates test scores
questions.explain: If test rows influence which features are chosen, the test score is no longer an honest estimate (data leakage).

questions.q: Mean voice minutes 401, median 338. The distribution is most likely:
questions.explain: A mean well above the median signals a few large values pulling the mean up.

questions.q: Which chart best shows whether leavers have shorter tenure than stayers, including spread and outliers?
options: Box plot of tenure by churn group
questions.explain: A box plot by group compares centre, spread and outliers at a glance.

questions.q: Match the question to the chart: “Do data used and monthly charge rise together?”
questions.explain: Two numeric variables together: scatter plot.

questions.q: 123 customers are recorded as exactly 18 years old, but only 23 as 19. An analyst should:
options: Flag it as a likely form default or minimum value and check with the data owner
questions.explain: EDA finds suspicious patterns and raises questions; it doesn’t silently ‘fix’ them.
